Building a Better 
Fellowship Pro￾gram
Over the past eighteen months we have run 
four cohorts of the fellowship, each with 
roughly forty participants drawn from gov￾ernment, industry and academia. The pro￾gram was designed to give mid-career pro￾fessionals a structured way into AI gover￾nance work, and the results have been en￾couraging, if not uniformly so.
This report summarises what we learned, 
what we would do differently, and where the 
fellowship should go next. It draws on par￾ticipant surveys, interviews with hiring or￾ganisations, and our own records of place￾ments and follow-on projects.
Key findings
Participants who completed a capstone 
project were twice as likely to change 
roles within six months.
Weekly facilitated discussions mattered 
more than reading volume; satisfaction 
fell sharply when groups exceeded 
eight people.
Employers valued the fellowship's network 
effects over its curriculum, which sur￾prised us.
Recommendations
Make the capstone mandatory and give 
every participant a mentor from a hir￾ing organisation.
Cap discussion groups at seven, and pay fa￾cilitators so that quality stays consis￾tent across cohorts.
Publish a short, honest impact report after 
every cohort, including the figures that 
flatter us least.
Finally, the fellowship's influence on partici￾pants' professional identity was its most sig￾nificant and least anticipated effect. Many 
told us that the official certificate was beside 
the point; what changed was their confi￾dence that this field had a place for them.
Our efficiency improved over time as well: 
the fourth cohort cost thirty percent less per 
participant than the first, mainly because of 
better-organised logistics and a flourishing 
alumni volunteer network.
